+# A shared state-tracing system
+
+## Status
+
+Planned and deliberately deferred. Decided on 2026-09-05: the compaction feature continues with its current
+JSONL trace, and this system is picked up later. Nothing here is a prerequisite for finishing the compaction gaps.
+
+The reason to write it down now is that the design constraints are freshest today than they will be then, and two
+of them were learned the expensive way: the hot-path write rule (below) and the "same name in every surface" rule.
+
+## Inventory
+
+Four stores already hold runtime state, each with its own format, lifetime, and reader:
+
+| store                                          | holds                                                                                                      | size now                   | bound                                                | reader                            |
+| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
+| `.state/compaction-trace.jsonl`                | one compaction's prefix verdict, per-stage attempt numbers, model answers, persisted summary, outcome      | 112 KB                     | 1 MB live + one `.1` generation, then silent discard | `scripts/compaction-report.mjs`   |
+| `.state/bash-log.jsonl` (sandbox decision log) | every allowed and blocked bash command with its decision, note, and outcome                                | 2.5 MB                     | 8 MB live + one `.1` generation                      | `npm run permission-report`       |
+| `.state/meta.sqlite`                           | agent workspaces, run instances, states, snapshots, results, continuation leases                           | 9.4 MB                     | unbounded; GC by age and byte budget                 | agent tool internals, TUI browser |
+| session `custom` entries                       | memory index snapshot, todo snapshots (up to 5.9 KB each), allowed-command rules (654 entries, max 9.5 KB) | in the 6.4 MB session file | session lifetime                                     | session readers, `pi` core        |
+
+Two of the four already rotate with the same hand-rolled logic (`rotateIfNeeded`, a `maxBytes` cap, a single `.1`
+generation, `fs.renameSync`). That duplication is the strongest argument for this system, and also the clearest
+statement of its minimum useful scope: **retention and reading, not event transport.**
+
+## What the store shape implies
+
+Both rotating files share a profile: metrics are cheap and bodies are not. 85.3% of the compaction trace's bytes
+were model response and persisted-summary text; the remaining 15% is what tells you anything, and it is about 200
+bytes per record. The bash log is the same story with commands instead of summaries.
+
+So the failure mode today is not unbounded growth - it is the opposite. The compaction trace accumulates
+100-200 KB per heavy development day, so the 1 MB cap discards everything past roughly a week, keeping exactly one
+previous generation and no way to protect a run worth studying. That is a design whose cost lands on the rare
+case we actually care about, and it is why "hold more, prune smarter" is the goal rather than "write somewhere
+else".
+
+## Goals
+
+1. One envelope, so a record from any producer answers the same four questions: when, from which process, from
+   which run or operation, and about which session.
+2. Retention as a declared property of a producer, not as code copy-pasted per module.
+3. One reader with a second format for machines, so a human report and an agent query are frontends over one
+   parsing path rather than two implementations that drift.
+4. Bounded growth with _graded_ decay: metrics kept for months, bodies for days, and a way to pin something so it
+   survives both.
+5. Transport that survives being wrong about the storage engine: the same records must be readable whether they
+   live in JSONL, gzip generations, or a database table.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- **Not an event bus.** Producers write records; nothing subscribes. In-process pub/sub is what `pi`'s hooks
+  already are, and duplicating them would create a second ordering problem to reason about.
+- **Not a replacement for the session file.** `custom` entries are durable _with_ the conversation and travel
+  with it; `.state/` is machine-local. Anything whose meaning depends on the session's history stays in the
+  session, and anything whose meaning depends on the process goes here.
+- **Not a metrics pipeline.** No aggregation daemon, no percentiles, no dashboards. Counts and thresholds over
+  recorded records have been enough so far, and they stay enough until a real question shows otherwise.
+- **Not backward-compatible forever.** Once every producer is on the envelope, older formats get one reader
+  branch and then a conversion, not permanent special cases.
+
+## Envelope
+
+Every record, whatever it carries:
+
+```jsonc
+{
+    "v": 1, // envelope version, bumped only on incompatible change
+    "ts": "2026-09-05T19:42:41.450Z",
+    "producer": "compaction", // stable id, one per registered producer
+    "kind": "prefix", // producer's own vocabulary
+    "run": "01a0...", // one operation: the correlation key
+    "session": "01a070e0-8e0",
+    "cwd": "/home/itterative/Repos/pi-coder",
+    "instance": "9c04a7", // per process load, see below
+    "payload": {/* kind-specific */},
+}
+```
+
+`instance` is a random id generated once per extension load and stamped on every record. It is the cheapest
+addition in this design and the one that pays best: it is what makes "did these two records come from the same
+chain, the same config, the same set of registered handlers?" a field comparison. The 2026-09-05 investigation
+turned on exactly this question and the data could not answer it, because records described a session and a time
+but not a process.
+
+Producers register as:
+
+```ts
+interface TraceProducer {
+    id: string;
+    kinds: { kind: string; retention: RetentionClass; description: string }[];
+}
+```
+
+Registration is the only coupling: the store never learns what a `prefix` record means, and producers never learn
+where their bytes go.
+
+## Retention classes
+
+Declared per kind, enforced in one place:
+
+| class    | kept                                                 | decay                                   | fits                                     |
+| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
+| `state`  | newest set only                                      | replace in place, bounded count         | snapshots, resolved config, rule sets    |
+| `metric` | months, or a byte budget in the thousands of records | never truncated                         | attempt numbers, verdicts, decisions     |
+| `body`   | days or newest N runs                                | drop the bytes, keep `chars` and `hash` | model answers, summaries, command output |
+| `pinned` | until unpinned                                       | exempt from all of the above            | anything worth debugging                 |
+
+The `body` decay is the important one and it is only expressible in a store that can update in place: the metrics
+around a large payload outlive the payload, so a run stays queryable and comparable after its text is gone. In
